I have a hypothetical question for you. The secon of these AI Max+ 395 128GB machines also contains an AI PRO R9700 32GB on it's 4-lane PCIe 4.0 bus. Is there any world where this can help
  improve the LLM throughput? Or is the PCIe bottleneck a dealbreaker?

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. content.text:
The dims come from the GGUF at load time, but for the math what matters is that the hidden state is a few KB per token — I have enough to answer concretely.

**Short answer: yes, it can genuinely help — but only in the configurations where weights never cross the bus. PCIe 4.0 x4 is a dealbreaker for streaming, and a non-issue for a static split.**

The bus is ~7 GB/s practical. Your iGPU reads unified memory at ~210-230 GB/s, and the R9700's GDDR6 runs at ~640 GB/s. So the two hard facts are:

1. **Any scheme that moves weights per token is dead on arrival.** Streaming even 10 GB of expert weights across the bus costs ~1.5 s/token. Same reason "use the dGPU as a prefill accelerator for iGPU-resident layers" doesn't work — prefill would starve at 7 GB/s.
2. **Any scheme that only moves activations is essentially free.** A hidden state is `NEmbd × 2-4 bytes` ≈ 4-16 KB per token per crossing. Even a speculative-decode verify batch of 8 tokens is ~100 KB — microseconds on the wire. The real per-crossing cost is submit/fence latency across two Vulkan devices (~50-300 µs), so the design rule is *few crossings per token*, not *few bytes*.

That points at three viable uses, in rough order of value:

**Contiguous layer split (pipeline).** Park a contiguous block of layers — up to ~28-30 GB after KV/scratch — resident on the R9700, the rest stays in unified memory. Two activation crossings per token. Decode is bandwidth-bound, so with a fraction *f* of per-token bytes served at 640 instead of ~220 GB/s, throughput scales as `1/(1−f+f·220/640)`. At *f* ≈ 0.35 (30 of 85 GB) that's ~1.30×, and prefill on those layers gets the R9700's much stronger RDNA4 compute too. Bonus: 30 GB of unified memory freed on a machine where the model currently eats 84-85 of 128 GB.

**KV cache + attention offload.** Long-context decode gets increasingly attention-bandwidth-bound; the KV cache and attention kernels can live entirely on the dGPU at 2.5× the bandwidth, with only Q in / attn-out back per token per layer. More crossings per token than the layer split though (one per attention layer unless you restructure), so sync latency needs care — the layer split gets the same bytes onto fast memory with 2 crossings instead of ~50.

**The MTP/spec-decode path you're already building.** The draft head could live on the R9700 and run ahead while the iGPU verifies, hiding draft latency entirely; the trunk hidden state it needs is a few KB. Smaller win than the layer split, but it composes with it.

What it costs you: real multi-device Vulkan plumbing — second `VkDevice`, no shared allocations, staging through host-visible memory (and note your write-combined-arena lesson applies double here: transfers must be device-side copies, never host reads of mapped dGPU memory). RADV supports Navi 48 fine.

One practical wrinkle: per your deployment plan, the LLM runs *alone* on one machine and the R9700 box hosts the other verticals. So exploiting this means either swapping which box runs the LLM or revisiting the split — worth deciding before investing in the multi-device work. The expected prize is roughly +30% decode and a bigger prefill win, which is meaningful but not transformative; I'd rank it below whatever's left on the spec-decode track for effort-per-token-per-second.

aiTitle: Evaluate PCIe bottleneck for dual GPU LLM throughput

content.text:
No — and your own p5c numbers show exactly why. There are two separate discounts between "70% acceptance" and realized speedup, and for this model the second one is the killer.

**Discount 1: acceptance gives you a ceiling of ×1.7, not ×1.7 realized.** With a single MTP draft token, each verify round emits the corrected token plus the draft *if* it's accepted: expected tokens per round = 1 + 0.7 = 1.7. So even with a literally free draft and a free verify, +70% is the *ceiling*, reached only if you draft every round.

**Discount 2: the 2-token verify round is not free, because this is a top-10-of-512 MoE.** In a dense model, verifying 2 tokens in one pass costs about the same as decoding 1, since the weight reads are shared — that's the whole trick of spec decode. But here two tokens route to essentially disjoint expert sets, so the expert reads (the bulk of your per-token bytes) nearly double. Your measured data quantifies it: in `p5c_spec_r1.csv`, the spec arm did 128 tokens in 87 rounds (1.47 tokens/round) at ~25 tok/s vs ~27.4 plain — which works out to a verify+draft round costing ~1.6× a plain decode step. Backing out the shared portion, that implies expert bytes are roughly 1.5× the shared dense/attention bytes per token.

Put together with a free draft: 1.7 tokens per round ÷ ~1.5-1.6× round cost ≈ **×1.05-1.15 — single-digit-to-modest percent, not 70%**. That's consistent with what you're seeing: at 64% measured acceptance you're currently *slower* than plain (24.6-26.9 vs 27.1-27.7 tok/s), because 1.47 tokens/round doesn't cover a 1.6× round cost.

Two caveats worth flagging:

- The "free 70%" premise itself is suspect on this codebase — the earlier `-mtp-free` run degenerated into a repetition loop that inflated acceptance by ~18 points. A free draft that scores 70% may be partly measuring the model agreeing with its own degenerate output.
- Drafting deeper doesn't rescue it here: k=2 raises the token ceiling to 1 + 0.7 + 0.49 = 2.19, but a 3-token verify reads ~3× the experts, so MoE spec decode has structurally worse returns than dense.

Where the leverage actually is: shrinking the round-cost ratio, not the acceptance. If the batch-2 verify could exploit expert overlap between the draft and the correction token (adjacent tokens do share some experts), or if the MoE GEMV batched two tokens through a shared expert working set more efficiently, the 1.6× comes down and the same 70% starts paying. The acceptance number was never the problem.
